prompt.context: Our client is Machine Co. – a European specialty machine manufacturer. The company researches, designs, and manufactures a variety of machines from underwater drills to semi-conductor chip fabricating machines. The machines are developed based on specific requirements of a customer, as well as brand products which are then marketed and sold to niche customers. One of Machine Co.'s brand products is an injection molding machine (XG43). This machine injects and molds plastic at high temperatures to create specific plastic products. XG43 is renowned for fabricating high quality products with a nine-sigma defect rate. The quality of products is unmatched by any other existing machine. Although XG43 has strong and profitable market share in Europe, it is unable to sell any machines in the US. Over the past few years, Machine Co. has made two unsuccessful attempts to penetrate the US market. McKinsey and Co. has been retained by Machine Co. to evaluate whether a third attempt is warranted, and if so, how can the attempt be made successful.
prompt.question: Should Machine Co. make a third attempt to enter the US market with XG43? If so, how should they approach it?

clarifying_info.q: Are we focusing only on XG43's potential in the US?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, for this discussion we are only going to focus on XG43's potential in the US.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have any information as to why Machine Co.'s previous two attempts at the US market were unsuccessful?
How should we measure success for this market entry?
clarifying_info.a: Market share and breakeven are reasonable success metrics.

framework: Understand XG43's value proposition: high quality (nine-sigma defect rate), and investigate additional value propositions such as efficiency/speed, power consumption, and material waste reduction

Understand the US market: size and segmentation of the injection molding machine market (low quality vs. high quality), identify US competitors, assess whether the value proposition is sufficient for customers to switch
Plan the market entry execution: brand awareness strategy, manufacturing location considerations, and critically the US service infrastructure required to support machines
Analyze the economics and breakeven: cost of service centers, XG43 price premium vs. current US machines, waste reduction savings for customers, and breakeven timeline

questions.prompt: What are XG43's value propositions beyond high quality?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies that in addition to the nine-sigma defect rate, XG43 reduces material waste by 10%. High efficiency/speed and low power consumption are NOT additional value propositions for this machine. The waste reduction is a critical insight worth 20% of the case.

questions.prompt: What is the key operational reason Machine Co.'s previous two US entry attempts failed, and what is needed to fix it?
questions.guidance: The root cause is the absence of US service infrastructure. When an injection molding machine breaks down it must be fixed immediately to avoid costly production losses, requiring a same-day on-site technician. Machine Co. has no US service presence. To successfully enter the US market, 10 service centers are required. Identifying this issue is worth 40% of the case.

questions.prompt: Calculate the customer breakeven: how long does it take a buyer of the XG43 to recoup the price premium over a standard US machine through waste savings?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify the price premium, then calculate annual savings from waste reduction, then divide to find breakeven. Target answer is approximately 2 years, which is within the 10-year machine life and supports the purchase decision. This calculation is worth 40% of the case.

math.setup: Price premium = XG43 price - current US machine price. Annual savings = waste reduced per day (lbs) x cost per lb x 365 days. Breakeven (years) = price premium / annual savings.
steps: Waste reduced per machine per day: 10% of 1 ton = 0.1 ton = 200 lbs
math.answer: Approximately 2 years to breakeven on the $300K price premium via waste reduction savings, well within the 10-year machine life.

questions.prompt: Assess the economics of the service center investment. Is the required service infrastructure financially justified?
questions.guidance: 10 service centers at $1M/year = $10M/year operating cost. Each year about 100 machines are ordered in the US; 10% (10 machines) are for high quality manufacturing — Machine Co.'s primary target. The $300K price premium across all machines sold generates substantial revenue to cover the $10M service cost. The service centers are a necessary investment and are financially justifiable once a meaningful number of machines are sold.

math.setup: Total annual service center cost = number of service centers x cost per center. Revenue from price premium = machines sold per year x price premium per machine.
steps: Annual service center cost: 10 centers x $1,000,000 = $10,000,000/year
High quality segment (primary target): 10% x 100 machines = 10 machines/year
Revenue from high quality segment alone: 10 x $300,000 = $3,000,000/year
If waste-reduction value prop also captures significant share of remaining 90 machines: 90 x $300,000 = $27,000,000/year potential
Total potential premium revenue: up to $30,000,000/year vs. $10,000,000/year service cost
math.answer: Service centers cost $10M/year. Even capturing only the 10 high-quality machines yields $3M — insufficient alone, but capturing a meaningful portion of the 90 waste-reduction buyers makes the infrastructure cost easily justifiable.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should Machine Co. consider when executing the US market entry?

categories.name: Service Infrastructure
ideas: Hire, train, and retain 10 service center technical staff across the US
Establish same-day response SLA to match European service levels
Determine optimal geographic placement of service centers to minimize response time

categories.name: Sales and Marketing
ideas: Develop a US-based sales force to educate customers on waste reduction ROI
Leverage rave reviews in industry journals and endorsements from independent agencies
Build a pipeline of pilot customers to generate US reference cases

categories.name: Pricing and Positioning
ideas: Maintain $450K price point to preserve European pricing parity
Create ROI calculators showing 2-year payback on waste reduction
Target the 10% high quality segment first as early adopters, then expand to waste-reduction buyers

categories.name: Regulatory and Compliance
ideas: Verify US regulatory requirements for industrial machinery
Ensure XG43 meets US safety and environmental standards

categories.name: Partnerships
ideas: Consider partnering with US distributors or equipment dealers for market access
Explore licensing or co-branding with an established US industrial brand

recommendation: Machine Co. should proceed with a third US market entry attempt for XG43
The two previous failures were caused by the absence of US service infrastructure — a solvable problem, not a fundamental market incompatibility

The value proposition is strong: XG43 serves the 10% high-quality segment directly, and the 10% waste reduction creates a ~2-year payback for the remaining 90% of buyers, well within the machine's 10-year life
risks: High upfront investment in 10 service centers ($10M/year) before revenue ramps
Difficulty hiring and retaining specialized technical staff in the US
Competitor response once Machine Co. announces US entry
Slower-than-expected customer adoption due to high price premium ($300K over existing machines)
next_steps: Hire, train, and deploy technical staff for 10 US service centers before or concurrent with first sales push
Develop a US-based sales organization to communicate the waste-reduction ROI to prospective buyers
Target the high-quality manufacturing segment (10 machines/year) first to build reference customers
Track market share and breakeven as primary success metrics
